candidates.title: Private-by-default turns
candidates.proposal:
Make every visitor’s turn private, so nobody must explain a problem publicly to obtain privacy. At the desk, one volunteer says: “You do not need to tell us why you came. We provide public information, not legal advice. Everyone can speak in the quiet corner when their turn comes.” Visitors wait in arrival order without giving names or case categories. The volunteer explains who is next by position, without announcing personal information. The second volunteer meets one visitor at a time in the quiet corner and begins with the printed service scope.

Visitors can read, point to, or ask for an oral explanation of existing materials. The volunteer asks only what is necessary to locate public information, interrupts unnecessary disclosure gently, and explains that individualized advice requires qualified help. Where existing materials identify qualified services, the volunteer points out their published contact or access instructions; otherwise, the limits of available referral information are stated plainly.

The mechanism is a universal private encounter: access to a quieter conversation never depends on revealing a sensitive reason. Implementation needs only the two volunteers, scope sheet, opening hours and corner. It assumes volunteers may operate away from the desk and that the corner offers adequate separation. A quiet corner may still be audible; volunteers must explain that limitation before details are shared. Arrival-order waiting also depends on a manageable queue.
candidates.experiment: Before opening, the volunteers alternate first-visitor role-play, comparing this flow with a simple desk welcome using the same materials. Include a visitor who prefers pointing and one who starts disclosing a case. Check whether each can identify the scope, waiting order and next step without public disclosure. Test speech audibility from the waiting position. During normal hours, tally navigation questions, uncertainty about turns and privacy complaints without recording case details or identifiers. If the corner is audible, visitors lose their place, or routine questions still require public explanation, the design needs revision. Role-play cannot establish real visitor comfort or qualified-service availability.

candidates.title: Visitor-controlled information route
candidates.proposal:
Let visitors choose their next action from the existing public materials before speaking to a volunteer. Place the printed scope where it can be read on approach, with opening hours and available information visibly arranged. One volunteer gives a consistent welcome: “You can browse without explaining anything, ask me to read the service information, or wait to speak in the quiet corner.” Browsing requires neither registration nor entry into a queue.

Visitors who find a relevant leaflet can take it if copies are available, or read it there. Those needing assistance join a single arrival-order queue without naming a subject. The second volunteer handles these requests in the corner, helping visitors locate and understand public information while declining individualized legal interpretation. Escalation uses qualified-help access instructions already present in the materials. Where these are absent, volunteers acknowledge that they cannot supply a verified destination from the available resources.

The primary mechanism is visitor control over disclosure and assistance: successful navigation can happen without a case conversation at all. This could reduce both exposure and demand for private turns. It requires readable, reasonably organized existing materials and volunteers who offer oral assistance without assuming literacy, language fluency or confidence. No new technology, intake form or specialist staffing is needed. Its principal limits are inaccessible materials, uncertainty about which leaflet applies, and visitors mistaking general information for advice. The welcome must therefore make assisted navigation and service limits explicit.
candidates.experiment: Use the same existing materials in two volunteer role-plays: their current arrangement with a simple welcome, then the proposed arrangement and three-choice welcome. Ask the acting visitor to find the service limits, locate available help and explain how to obtain private assistance. Include a scenario where no leaflet answers the question. Failure occurs if browsing leads to an unsupported conclusion, help requires naming a case publicly, or the visitor cannot find the private route. During normal operation, use anonymous tallies of completed navigation, repeated waiting questions and privacy complaints; optionally ask departing visitors whether they found their next step. Any comparison is preliminary because visitor needs and traffic vary.

candidates.title: Orientation before questions
candidates.proposal:
Give every newcomer the same brief, case-free orientation before inviting any questions. One volunteer explains the opening hours, what the desk can and cannot do, how waiting works, the option to use the quiet corner, and how qualified-help information is located in the existing printed materials. The opening sentence is: “Please keep personal details for a quieter conversation; you do not need to explain your situation here.” If several people arrive together, they may hear the same orientation, with no introductions or requests to describe their needs. Late arrivals receive their own explanation rather than waiting for a scheduled session.

After orientation, visitors can read public materials, leave with an available leaflet, or wait in arrival order for the second volunteer in the corner. Public questions are limited to service logistics. If a visitor begins describing a case, the volunteer redirects gently to the private turn without repeating the details. In the corner, volunteers explain public information and its limits; requests for advice are directed to qualified-help instructions already available in print. No referral destination or appointment availability is assumed.

The mechanism is anticipatory explanation: visitors learn the boundaries and sequence before trying to gain attention through personal disclosure. It uses volunteer speech and existing materials, so it can assist visitors who cannot comfortably read the scope sheet. It assumes the welcome can be heard and understood without disrupting private conversations. Language barriers, hearing needs and a busy arrival stream may limit its effectiveness; individual repetition remains necessary.
candidates.experiment: Have the volunteers alternate newcomer role-play, comparing the standard orientation with simply offering the scope sheet. After each, ask the acting visitor to explain what happens next, whether details are needed publicly, and where advice requests go. Check from the corner whether the welcome masks or exposes conversation. During existing opening hours, anonymously tally wrong-next-step attempts, questions about waiting and privacy complaints, alongside an optional departure question about finding a next step. The mechanism is weakened if visitors still start case accounts to secure a turn or cannot explain the queue. Staff role-play checks clarity only; real visitor comprehension and comfort remain uncertain until observed.
